verifiedClaims.claim: Why Ashley Phosphate & I-26 Is the Tri-County's Highest-Crash Intersection
verifiedClaims.currentValue: 2024 (latest SCDPS edition): I-26 at S-75 (Ashley Phosphate Road) had 174 collisions — 0 fatal, 1 serious-injury, 25 other-injury, 148 property-damage-only; 0 killed, 1 seriously injured, 38 other injuries (39 injured). Rank: 2nd in Charleston County behind I-26 at US-78 (190 collisions, 0 fatal); Berkeley's top intersection was I-26 at S-62/College Park Rd (113) and Dorchester's was US-78 at SC-165 (56), so 2nd in the tri-county. Statewide, 5th: behind I-85 at S-492 (Greenville, 277), I-20 at US-176 (Richland, 224), I-85 at SC-290 (Spartanburg, 199) and I-26 at US-78 (Charleston, 190). For 2011–2015 the Post and Courier's SCDPS analysis did rank it No. 1 in the tri-county (629 crashes).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: SCDPS Office of Highway Safety and Justice Programs, South Carolina Traffic Collision Fact Book 2024 Edition (latest), Part VI county tables: Charleston County p. 105, Berkeley County p. 101, Dorchester County p. 121
verifiedClaims.note: NOT a patcher-editable surface (title is not in body.html) — for the owner. The present-tense superlative was true for 2011–2015 only. In 2024 it was #2 in Charleston County and the tri-county (174 vs 190 at I-26/US-78). Suggested title: "Why Ashley Phosphate & I-26 Is One of the Tri-County's Highest-Crash Intersections" (or keep the superlative but date it: "...Was the Tri-County's Highest-Crash Intersection, 2011–2015"). The Fact Book has no single statewide intersection table; the statewide rank is derived from all 46 county Top-5 tables and is exact because every county's 5th-place intersection had fewer than 174 collisions (max 122). S-75 = Ashley Phosphate Road per SCDOT's Charleston County AADT sheet ('I-26 S-75 (ASHLEY PHOSPHATE RD) TO S-1342 (AVIATION AV)'); S-62 in Berkeley = College Park Road (same sheet). The Fact Book notes intersections are based on officer-reported route numbers, so the 'I-26 at S-75' count is the interchange as coded on crash reports.

Replace: "Government entities like SCDOT may share liability for a malfunctioning or defective traffic signal they failed to fix after notice — but not for highway design — under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act, which has a two-year deadline (S.C. Code §§ 15-78-60(15), 15-78-110)."

verifiedClaims.claim: A Post and Courier analysis of 2011–2015 collision data recorded 629 crashes at the Ashley Phosphate Road and I-26 intersection — roughly one every three days. That was more than at any other intersection in Berkeley, Charleston or Dorchester counties, and second in the state behind I-20 at US-176 in Columbia.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: 2024 (latest SCDPS edition): I-26 at S-75 (Ashley Phosphate Road) had 174 collisions — 0 fatal, 1 serious-injury, 25 other-injury, 148 property-damage-only; 0 killed, 1 seriously injured, 38 other injuries (39 injured). Rank: 2nd in Charleston County behind I-26 at US-78 (190 collisions, 0 fatal); Berkeley's top intersection was I-26 at S-62/College Park Rd (113) and Dorchester's was US-78 at SC-165 (56), so 2nd in the tri-county. Statewide, 5th: behind I-85 at S-492 (Greenville, 277), I-20 at US-176 (Richland, 224), I-85 at SC-290 (Spartanburg, 199) and I-26 at US-78 (Charleston, 190).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Post and Courier, Robert Behre, "What are the tri-county's 10 most dangerous intersections?" (Mar. 4, 2017; updated Sept. 14, 2020), citing preliminary SCDPS data — Internet Archive capture of 2025-03-29
verifiedClaims.note: FAQPage structured data. Historical figures verified; add the current year so the answer is not stale: "In 2024, the latest state data, it recorded 174 collisions — about one every two days — second in the tri-county and fifth statewide (SCDPS)."

verifiedClaims.claim: Worth noting alongside the frequency: none of those 629 crashes was fatal, though 181 people were injured.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Post and Courier, Robert Behre, "What are the tri-county's 10 most dangerous intersections?" (Mar. 4, 2017; updated Sept. 14, 2020), citing preliminary SCDPS data — Internet Archive capture of 2025-03-29
verifiedClaims.note: Verified.

verifiedClaims.claim: Five primary factors: vehicles exiting I-26 at highway speed encountering a red light within a short distance, complex left-turn movements across multiple lanes, commercial density on all four corners generating constant turning conflicts, long signal cycles that encourage red-light running, and traffic volume that far exceeds the intersection's design capacity.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: SCDOT (Board 3): high volumes and numerous conflicting turning movements; Ashley Phosphate volumes exceed the recommended level for two-way left-turn lanes. I-26: 170,500 vehicles/day (2025 AADT).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: SCDOT Ashley Phosphate Road Safety Improvements, Board 3; SCDOT Average Daily Traffic for Charleston County, 2025 AADT (generated 2026-03-13), stations 2189, 2191, 440; 2024 sheet for comparison
verifiedClaims.note: FAQPage structured data. Drop the unsourced 'long signal cycles that encourage red-light running' and 'on all four corners'. Suggested: "Several factors: vehicles leaving I-26 meet a signal shortly after exiting, left turns cross three lanes of opposing traffic, businesses along Ashley Phosphate Road create constant turning conflicts, and volume is heavy — about 170,000 vehicles a day on I-26 beside the interchange and 65,000 on Ashley Phosphate Road (SCDOT, 2025)."

verifiedClaims.claim: Under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act, the city of North Charleston and SCDOT may bear liability for intersection design deficiencies they knew or should have known about.
verifiedClaims.note: FAQPage structured data. Contradicted: the TCA bars liability for highway design; the notice standard applies to the 'absence, condition, or malfunction' of signs and signals. Replace: "Under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act, SCDOT or another responsible agency may be liable when a traffic signal or sign was missing, defective or malfunctioning and was not fixed within a reasonable time after the agency knew or should have known — but agencies are not liable for the design of highways (S.C. Code § 15-78-60(15))."

verifiedClaims.claim: Given the well-documented crash data at Ashley Phosphate/I-26, a strong argument exists that the responsible agencies have been on notice of the danger.
verifiedClaims.note: Crash-frequency notice does not overcome design immunity; 'strong argument' overstates. Delete.

verifiedClaims.claim: These claims require strict notice compliance — contact an attorney promptly.
verifiedClaims.note: No pre-suit notice is mandatory: a verified claim 'may be filed' (within one year) and extends the deadline to three years; otherwise suit within two years. Replace: "These claims have a shorter deadline — two years, or three if a verified claim is filed with the agency within one year — and damages are capped, so contact an attorney promptly."

verifiedClaims.claim: Call 911 for a police report, seek immediate medical attention at Trident Medical Center, photograph the scene (including signal positions and vehicle locations), get witness contact information, do not give recorded statements to insurance companies, and contact a personal injury attorney who can preserve traffic camera footage and signal timing data before it is overwritten.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Trident Health — Trident Hospital location page
verifiedClaims.note: Advice; Trident is the nearest trauma center (Level II). Optional: 'at Trident Medical Center or the nearest emergency room' so the FAQ does not imply a single required hospital. If the post adds report advice, the SC crash report is form TR-310 (not FR-10).

Suggested title: "Why Ashley Phosphate & I-26 Is One of the Tri-County's Highest-Crash Intersections". Slug change needs a 301.

Intro + Numbers list: keep the 2011–2015 P&C figures with explicit dating ('ranked second for 2011–2015'); replace the lone 'Injury severity' bullet with the 2024 SCDPS line (174 collisions, 0 killed, 39 injured, 148 PDO; #2 tri-county, #5 statewide). Delete the invented '7-10 days' benchmark sentences.
'so deadly' (intro sentence and H2 '5 Reasons This Intersection Is So Deadly') → 'so crash-prone' / 'Sees So Many Crashes'.

Fixes list: red-light camera bullet → FHWA ~25% fewer right-angle / ~15% more rear-end, and SC bars local camera ticketing (§ 56-5-710). Replace 'Grade separation' bullet (already an interchange) with the SCDOT raised-median project (groundbreaking July 2025). Replace 'the question is whether they will act' with SCDOT's 2025 project.

Owner confirm: 'handled dozens of cases from the Ashley Phosphate/I-26 intersection' and 'handle crash cases from this intersection regularly' (firm-experience claims).

statuteCitations.name: Three-year limitation: (5) personal injury; (6) wrongful death from date of death
Minors — tolling during minority, no more than one year after age 18 (applies to Ch. 78 actions too; not on page)
Tort Claims Act exception — signs/signals liability only after notice; no liability for the design of highways
Verified claim may be filed; if filed, within one year of discovery of loss
Tort Claims Act limitation — two years, three if a claim was first filed
Tort Claims Act damages caps — $300,000 per person / $600,000 per occurrence

Joint and several liability — a defendant under 50% of total fault pays only its share; 2025 Act 42 (eff. Jan. 1, 2026) compares fault of all defendants and tortfeasors, not just named defendants (not on page; reference)
Local authorities may not issue tickets based on photographic (camera) evidence
Photo-evidence citations limited to declared emergencies; in-person service within one hour
Evidence of a traffic conviction is inadmissible in a civil action (not on page; reference)
